name: Umar Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Umar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for companies, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the admin team at a letting agency with three branches, so me and two others handle tenancy agreements, deposit paperwork, repair bookings, landlord statements and the viewing diary. I use AI every day: it drafts the tenancy paperwork from our templates, sorts the repair emails by urgency, and I built a little system that answers the common tenant questions overnight. I like fixing processes. Give me a messy spreadsheet and I'm happy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay's lower than in the city, and I've got less than a month saved because I live on my own in a studio above a launderette and the rent's most of my wage. There aren't many office jobs like this in town, so I can't be choosy. And tenants shout at you when their boiler's broken, which I get, but it's still not fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and people expected too much. At the branch I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd post the odd tip in an admin forum I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's safe and I'm a bit ahead of everyone else. But I'm still on lower pay, my rent's still most of my wage, and the agency's margins are thin, so a raise isn't guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a promotion to office manager across all three branches, with my systems as the pitch. I'd keep improving the overnight question system. And I'd try to save a hundred a month by cooking more and cutting the takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've built systems already. What would you do with the time they save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take on more of the landlord side, statements and renewals, so I'm doing higher-value work. A tool that saves me two hours is only useful if my manager sees what I did with the two hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressure is there on you regardless of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, mainly. If the landlord puts it up again in spring, I'm in trouble. And the agency's lost two big landlords this year, so the owner's watching every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ahead, not complain. At work I'd be the one running the rollout. Online I'd share what's working, because I think people should see real examples, not headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the admin team goes from three to one, and I plan to be the one. I'd be anxious if I wasn't already doing it, but I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the owner with a plan: automate deposits, statements and repair booking across all branches, and make me operations lead. I'd learn the property software properly and do a lettings qualification online, so I can also do viewings and inspections. That's the bit that still needs legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly positive. Underneath it, a bit nervous, because I like the two people I work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your two team members, what happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia would probably move to a negotiator job, she's great with tenants. Tom's younger and would struggle. I'd try to get the owner to keep him on for viewings at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're automating yourself out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's always a risk. But if someone's going to automate my job, I'd rather it was me, so at least I'm the one who knows how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick and nobody's ready, me included. At work I'd be practical: let's get the systems in, but keep people on the property side. I'd tell friends to save whatever they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the admin and operations work goes almost straight away, including mine. Being good at the tools doesn't help when the tools run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into property management in the first year, doing inspections, check-ins and dealing with contractors on site. I'd learn basic maintenance so I'm useful in person. And I'd cut my costs hard, maybe move into a shared flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel like I can move, but it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. Where does a letting agency end up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it is thinking work, so it shrinks fast. But someone still has to stand in a flat and check the damp, meet a plumber, hand over keys. For three years that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got under a month saved. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd swap the studio for a room in a shared house, and keep a hundred aside from every pay. A month of savings is nothing when your whole job could change in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, so use it. At work I'd push the owner to plan, not wait. I'd keep sharing tips online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can build the operations role for a couple of years, then step into property management before AGI. That's a decent path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the lettings qualification this year, then a part-time building surveying course. I'd keep improving the agency's systems so I'm paid a bit more meanwhile. And I'd save every raise instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two or three years earning more as operations lead, then a surveying qualification by the time thinking AI arrives. A surveyor still has to climb into the loft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just starting in admin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't get comfortable at a desk. Learn the bit of the job where you have to be in the room.

I'd push the owner to **plan**, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're not lazy. At work I'd encourage everyone to pick something hands-on to learn. I'd stay practical online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly opportunity. I'd have time to become a surveyor properly and still enjoy the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency job and grow into operations. I'd start the surveying course around 2028. I'd save steadily and maybe, once I had a cushion, rent a slightly better flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Motivated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper career. Operations, then surveying, maybe my own small property management business later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Ten years sounds like forever, which is exactly why people waste it. I'd set myself a target year for each step.

I'd encourage colleagues to learn something **hands-on**.
think: I have time to become **a surveyor** properly.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, which is exactly why people waste it.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his plan into **a career ladder**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm quick with this stuff and even I'd be scrambling. What would help is cheap, fast courses in hands-on property skills, and some rent help for people retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me get paid for the change we drive. I've saved the agency hours every week, and my pay hasn't moved in two years.

headlineQuote: I've saved the agency hours every week, and my pay hasn't moved in two years.

He lives alone in a **studio** with under a month saved and rent eating his wage.
He sees himself as the **driver of automation**, aiming for operations lead.
Under faster AGI he moves into **property management** and surveying, the in-person side.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even he would be scrambling.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap fast **hands-on property** courses and **rent help** for people retraining.
